The draft is in good shape. Each paragraph does a different job (problem, cause, decision, result, cost), and nothing repeats across sections. I made no changes to the file.

## Structural notes

1. **The evidence is vaguer than the claim.** "Most of our worst outages started on a Friday" and "Incidents dropped a lot after the freeze" are the whole case, and they are the two vaguest sentences in the post. This is the single change that matters most.
   - Fact needed from the writer: how many of the worst outages started on a Friday, and out of how many?
   - Fact needed from the writer: how many incidents were there before and after the March freeze, and over what period?

2. **Paragraph 2 promises one reason and gives two.** "Friday deploys fail for a dull reason" introduces the handoff problem: the authors go home. Then the release tool that batches the week's deploys shows up as a second, separate cause. A sharp reader will ask why you froze Fridays and did not fix the batching. Say "two reasons" at the start, and answer that question.
   - Fact needed from the writer: did the batching change after the freeze, and why was the fix a freeze and not a change to the release tool?

3. **The longer Monday queue appears twice.** Paragraph 4 says "the Monday queue got longer". Paragraph 5 says the same cost with a better example. Keep it in one place. Paragraph 5 is the stronger home.

## Line notes

Safe cuts, where the idea stays in the text elsewhere:

- "It is important to note that" is throat-clearing. Start at "Most of our worst outages started on a Friday."
- "each and every" is a doublet. Use "every".
- "Weekends got quieter" restates "Incidents dropped" in softer words. Cut it, or merge it into the number.
- "which we expected" tells the reader nothing. Cut the clause.
- "put it plainly" announces the quote. "Ana said" is sufficient.

Rewrites, not cuts, because each sentence links its neighbours:

- "The pattern was hard to miss once we read the incident log." This repeats the sentence before it, but it is the only place that names the source. Move the incident log into the claim: "The incident log shows most of our worst outages started on a Friday."
- "This made rollbacks slower." "This" has no noun, but the sentence carries the consequence that "So in March" answers. Name the cause: "Not knowing which change broke production made rollbacks slower."
  - Fact needed from the writer: how much slower, in minutes or hours?
- "The freeze has a cost." This announces the paragraph, but it also makes the turn from result to cost. Keep the turn and put the cost in it: "The freeze costs us something: a fix that is ready at two on Friday waits until Monday morning."

Smaller points:

- "one Friday train" is jargon that an outside reader may not know. "One Friday release" is plainer.
- "some weeks that delay annoys a customer" is soft and hedged.
  - Fact needed from the writer: one real delayed fix, and what it cost the customer or how frequently this occurs.

## Do not cut these

- "When something breaks at nine on Saturday, the on-call engineer has to read an unfamiliar diff before deciding whether to roll back." This is the best sentence in the post.
- Ana's quote, "I would rather ship on Monday than debug on Sunday."
- "So in March we froze deploys after noon on Friday."
- The last sentence. It makes the trade-off and ties back to the unfamiliar diff.
- "Nobody argued." The two passes disagreed on this one. The whole-document pass called it a fragment for effect. The line pass called it a plain fact. I report it as a keep, because it lands the quote.

Most of the line notes are safe tightening, and `tighten` can apply them. The three structural notes need facts that only you have.
artifact.draft.md:
# Why we stopped deploying on Fridays

For two years our team shipped whenever a change was ready, Friday afternoons included. It is important to note that most of our worst outages started on a Friday. The pattern was hard to miss once we read the incident log.

Friday deploys fail for a dull reason. The people who wrote the change go home, and the people on call over the weekend did not write it. When something breaks at nine on Saturday, the on-call engineer has to read an unfamiliar diff before deciding whether to roll back. Our release tool also batched each and every deploy from the week into one Friday train, and the on-call engineer could not tell which change had broken production. This made rollbacks slower.

So in March we froze deploys after noon on Friday. In the retro, Ana put it plainly: "I would rather ship on Monday than debug on Sunday." Nobody argued.

Incidents dropped a lot after the freeze. Weekends got quieter, and the Monday queue got longer, which we expected.

The freeze has a cost. A fix that is ready at two on Friday waits until Monday morning, and some weeks that delay annoys a customer. We decided that cost is smaller than a weekend spent reading someone else's code.

**9 line notes, 4 structural. Biggest: the piece claims "most of our worst outages" and "dropped a lot" and gives no number for either.**

The file is unchanged.

## Structural notes

1. **The result has no number.** "Incidents dropped a lot after the freeze" is the payoff of the piece, and it is an adjective. "Weekends got quieter" then says the same thing again in softer words.
   - Fact needed from the writer: how many incidents before the freeze and after it, and over what period?

2. **The opening claim has no number either.** "Most of our worst outages started on a Friday" carries the whole case.
   - Fact needed from the writer: how many outages, and how many of them started on a Friday?

3. **The trade-off appears three times.** Ana's quote makes it, "the Monday queue got longer, which we expected" makes it again, and the last paragraph makes it a third time.
   - Safe cut: "and the Monday queue got longer, which we expected". The last paragraph states the same cost with a better example.
   - Conditional: the closing sentence, "We decided that cost is smaller than a weekend spent reading someone else's code." The whole-document pass says it duplicates Ana's quote and that one of the two must go. The line pass calls it a good ending, and calls the quote the best line in the piece. The quote is the motive at the time of the decision and the closer is the verdict after the cost is known, so this is not a plain duplicate. Whether to cut it depends on what the piece is for.

4. **The second cause is attached with "also."** The batched Friday release is a real second reason, separate from "the author went home." Say plainly that there are two reasons.
   - Fact needed from the writer: is the batching a separate cause, or is the "Friday train" the same thing as the Friday deploys the paragraph opens with?

**The single change that matters most:** put the count of Friday outages in the first paragraph, and the incident counts from before and after the freeze in the fourth.

## Word and sentence notes

- **"It is important to note that"** is throat-clearing. Cut it and start at "Most of our worst outages…"
- **"The pattern was hard to miss once we read the incident log."** This repeats the sentence before it, but it also names the source of the claim. Shorten it and keep the source: "The incident log showed it."
- **"each and every"** is a doublet. Use "every."
- **"one Friday train"** is jargon. "One Friday release" says the same thing.
- **"people on call" and "on-call engineer"** are two names for one thing. Use "on-call engineer" throughout.
- **"This made rollbacks slower."** "This" has no noun, and the sentence restates the clause before it. Fold it in: "…could not tell which change had broken production, so rollbacks took longer."
  - Fact needed from the writer: how much slower, if known?
- **"Ana put it plainly:"** is padding, because the quote is already plain. Use "Ana said."
- **"The freeze has a cost."** It announces the point before it states it, but it also carries the turn from the results to the cost. Rewrite so the turn survives, for example "But a fix that is ready at two on Friday waits until Monday morning."
- **"some weeks that delay annoys a customer"** is vague.
  - Fact needed from the writer: how often did this happen, or what is one real case?

The two passes disagree on "Nobody argued." One says cut it as a fragment for effect. The other says it reports a fact and works.

## Lines to keep

- "When something breaks at nine on Saturday, the on-call engineer has to read an unfamiliar diff before deciding whether to roll back." This is the most concrete sentence and it carries the argument.
- "So in March we froze deploys after noon on Friday."
- Ana's quote.
- The example of the fix that is ready at two on Friday.

The order of the piece (problem, cause, decision, result, cost) is right. Most of the word-level notes are safe tightening, and `tighten` will apply them, but the four missing numbers can only come from you.

**10 line notes, 2 structural. Biggest: the two claims the post depends on have no numbers.**

I did not change the file.

## Structural

**1. The proof and the result have no figures.** This is the change that matters most. "Most of our worst outages started on a Friday" is the reason for the freeze. "Incidents dropped a lot after the freeze" is the result. A skeptical reader cannot weigh either one. The draft says you read the incident log, so the figures exist.
- Fact needed from the writer: how many of the worst outages started on a Friday, and out of how many?
- Fact needed from the writer: how many incidents were there before and after the March freeze, and over what period?

**2. The second cause is not tied to Friday.** Paragraph 2 gives two causes: the on-call engineer did not write the change, and the release tool put the week's deploys into one batch. Batching would hurt on any day. Either say that batching made the Friday problem worse, or cut it. This is a decision about content, so it is yours. Deirdre leans toward keeping it.

No section opens by restating the title, and no paragraph closes by restating itself. The last sentence repeats the idea of paragraph 2, but it states the decision, so it stays.

## Line notes

- **"It is important to note that"**: throat-clearing. Start at "Most of our worst outages started on a Friday." Safe cut.
- **"each and every"**: redundant pair. Use "every." Safe cut.
- **"The pattern was hard to miss once we read the incident log."**: it says the pattern was clear but does not show it. Do not cut it, because it is the only place that names the incident log. Fold it into the sentence before: "When we read the incident log, we saw that most of our worst outages started on a Friday."
- **"This made rollbacks slower."**: "This" has no noun, and the sentence before already shows the engineer could not find the bad change. Deirdre would cut it. I report it as a rewrite, because "So in March we froze deploys" depends on this conclusion. Join it to the sentence before with "so."
  - Fact needed from the writer: how much slower were rollbacks?
- **"also batched … and the on-call engineer could not tell"**: the second half is the result of the first, but "and" hides that. Use "so."
- **"Friday train"**: a term the reader has not seen. Say "one Friday release," or define it.
- **"the people on call over the weekend" / "the on-call engineer"**: two names for one role in adjacent sentences. Use one.
- **"Ana put it plainly"**: it announces the quote. "Ana said" is enough. The quote itself stays word for word. "Retro" is jargon for an outside reader.
- **"Weekends got quieter, and the Monday queue got longer, which we expected."**: "which" can point at either clause. Say what was expected. Also say what is in the queue.
  - Fact needed from the writer: how much longer did the Monday queue get?
- **"some weeks that delay annoys a customer"**: vague. Keep it and sharpen it.
  - Fact needed from the writer: what happened to a customer when a fix waited, or how often does it happen?

## Where the two passes disagree

- **"Friday deploys fail for a dull reason."** The line pass says "dull" is a wink and wants the reason stated directly. The whole-document pass says keep it, because it sets up the paragraph.
- **"The freeze has a cost."** The line pass says it is direct and good. The whole-document pass says it announces the paragraph and does not state the cost. It is the sentence that turns the post from results to cost, so if you change it, the turn must stay.

## Keep as written

- "When something breaks at nine on Saturday, the on-call engineer has to read an unfamiliar diff before deciding whether to roll back." Both passes call this the best sentence in the draft.
- "So in March we froze deploys after noon on Friday."
- "Nobody argued."
- "A fix that is ready at two on Friday waits until Monday morning."
- The whole cost paragraph. Do not trim it to make the post look more positive.

Most of the line notes are safe tightening, and `/draft:tighten` applies those. The two structural notes need your figures first.
